newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian job woes add weight to fifth rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australian job woes add weight to fifth rate cut.

text.p: Australia's ailing labour market was delivered another blow on Thursday as news of the largest fall in employment for over four years put the prospect of a fifth cut in interest rates firmly on the agenda.
Employment fell by 40,300 in May, the largest fall since April 1993, and well below median forecasts of a 15,000 rise, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed.
Unemployment rose to 8.8 percent, stopped from breaching 9.0 percent only by a drop in the number of people looking for work, presumably discouraged by high unemployment, analysts said.
"It's a very disturbing number," ABN-Amro chief economist Susan Creighton said. "It certainly increase the chances of an interest rate cut."

If the Reserve Bank of Australia were to cut rates from the current level of 5.50 percent, it would be the fifth time since last July. Economists said the run of data since the last cut on May 23 had not only supported that decision but suggested the economy was still in need of a further boost.
The market certainly began to think a cut was on the agenda, and that it could come at any time ahead of the RBA's next board meeting on July 1.
The dollar dropped half a cent to a 16 month low of US$0.7510 soon after the data on the prospect of a rate cut, while bonds and bills rallied sharply on the news.

June 10-year bond futures rallied to a high 17 points above their close on the news, while September bill futures rallied over 20 points to an implied yield of 5.23 percent, over a quarter of a percent under the current cash rate.

"Everyone's going to be watching their screens very nervously for the next two weeks," ANZ Treasury senior economist David de Garis said, referring to the 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT) announcement time for RBA policy change announcements.
The May fall followed a strong 37,100 rise in April jobs, and economists said given the data's volatility a rise was likely in June, but there was little disguising a very weak trend.
"We may see some improvement, but improvement from zero to 10,000 jobs for a month still wouldn't be enough to get the unemployment rate down," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.

The continued weakness in full-time employment remains a concern. Full-time jobs fell 23,100 in May, and are now down 17,600 over the past year. Put another way, the economy has lost almost 1,500 full-time jobs per month over the last year.
The only growth that has come has been in part-time work, and even that has been weak, rising only 69,500 over the past year.
All up, employment has risen by 51,900 in the year to May, at an average of just 4,325 jobs per month.
Against that, some economists felt that while weak, the labour market was only reflecting a weak economy in late 1996.

"The point I would make and very strongly is that employment growth is a lagging indicator in our economy, so even the strength we saw in quarter one won't show up in better employment until we get to quarter three or quarter four," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
